identification.summary: Clay Typhoon is a Microsoft designation for a China-nexus actor; public reporting found here describes it only through vendor crosswalks rather than a Microsoft write-up [S1][S2]. Volexity's June 2026 reporting links Clay Typhoon (Microsoft) with its own VerdantBamboo cluster, Google's UNC5221 and CrowdStrike's Warp Panda, all associated with the BRICKSTORM backdoor used for long-term espionage access to VMware, storage and network appliances that typically lack EDR [S1][S2][S5].
identification.firstObserved: No Microsoft first-observed date located. CrowdStrike says Warp Panda has been active since at least 2022 [S4]; the CISA-investigated BRICKSTORM intrusion began in April 2024 [S6]; Volexity's VerdantBamboo intrusion lasted at least 18 months before discovery in September 2025 [S1].
identification.notes: Storm-2416 is the Microsoft in-development name already held in this record (from Microsoft's naming table, which could not be opened in this pass). Overlaps: Volexity states VerdantBamboo is tracked by Microsoft as Clay Typhoon, by Google as UNC5221 and by CrowdStrike as Warp Panda [S1][S2]. These are overlapping vendor clusters, not proven identical sets; facts below are attributed to the vendor that reported them. GTIG says UNC5221 is often reported as Silk Typhoon but GTIG does not consider the two the same cluster [S5].

attribution.sponsor: People's Republic of China (state-sponsored per US/Canadian government reporting on BRICKSTORM operators) [S6]. No source located names the specific PRC service behind Clay Typhoon.
attribution.confidence: Microsoft's own confidence statement for Clay Typhoon was not located. CrowdStrike describes Warp Panda as a China-nexus adversary whose access likely supports intelligence collection aligned with China's strategic interests [S3][S4]. Google GTIG tracks UNC5221 as a suspected China-nexus cluster [S5]. CISA, NSA and the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security attribute BRICKSTORM use to PRC state-sponsored actors, without using the Clay Typhoon name [S6]. The Clay Typhoon to VerdantBamboo/UNC5221/Warp Panda mapping rests on Volexity's reporting as relayed by secondary coverage [S1][S2].
attribution.basis: Vendor tradecraft and malware overlaps (BRICKSTORM family, appliance targeting) across Volexity, Google, CrowdStrike and joint government reporting [S1][S3][S5][S6].

objectives: Long-term covert espionage access; CrowdStrike assesses Warp Panda's persistence likely supports intelligence collection aligned with PRC strategic interests [S4]. Google assesses UNC5221 targeting of legal and technology firms and SaaS providers may support zero-day development and access to downstream customers [S5].

targeting.notes: Sector and region data come from the overlapping clusters (Warp Panda, UNC5221, VerdantBamboo) and from government BRICKSTORM reporting; none was located in a Microsoft Clay Typhoon publication [S1][S3][S5][S6].

capabilities.summary: BRICKSTORM is a Go-based ELF backdoor aimed at VMware vCenter and ESXi that blends C2 into HTTPS/WebSocket traffic and uses DNS-over-HTTPS; operators stole cloned VM snapshots for credential extraction, created hidden rogue VMs, and in one CISA case compromised ADFS and exported cryptographic keys [S6]. Google reports deployment on appliances without EDR (network storage, vCenter, remote access appliances), average dwell time of 393 days, and at least one case of Ivanti Connect Secure zero-day exploitation for access [S5]. CrowdStrike reports Warp Panda used Golang implants Junction (ESXi) and GuestConduit (guest VM tunneling), pivoted from internet-facing edge devices into vCenter with valid credentials or vCenter CVEs (e.g., CVE-2024-38812, CVE-2023-34048, CVE-2021-22005), and abused Ivanti (CVE-2024-21887, CVE-2023-46805) and F5 BIG-IP (CVE-2023-46747) flaws [S3][S4]. Volexity reports a FreeBSD BRICKSTORM variant on a pfSense firewall, the .NET Core backdoor PLENET (aka GRIMBOLT) and the Python reverse shell AGENTPSD, plus local privilege escalation on an Egnyte Storage Sync appliance [S1][S2].

campaigns.name: Warp Panda VMware vCenter intrusions (CrowdStrike)
campaigns.summary: CrowdStrike reports Warp Panda active since at least 2022 against US legal, technology and manufacturing entities, compromising vCenter/ESXi with BRICKSTORM, Junction and GuestConduit; one intrusion began in late 2023 [S3][S4].

campaigns.name: CISA-investigated BRICKSTORM intrusion (AR25-338A)
campaigns.summary: PRC state-sponsored actors gained persistent access in April 2024, placed BRICKSTORM on an internal vCenter server and compromised ADFS; joint CISA/NSA/Canadian Centre report released 4 December 2025 (actor not named Clay Typhoon) [S6].

campaigns.name: VerdantBamboo MSP pivot to appliances (Volexity)
campaigns.summary: Volexity found during a September 2025 response an intrusion of at least 18 months that came through the victim's managed service provider, deployed a FreeBSD BRICKSTORM variant on a pfSense firewall, used Egnyte Storage Sync local privilege escalation, PLENET and AGENTPSD, and saw the actor return using stolen firewall credentials; published June 2026 [S1][S2].

campaigns.name: BRICKSTORM espionage campaign (Google GTIG / UNC5221)
campaigns.summary: Google tracked activity from March 2025 against US legal, SaaS, BPO and technology organizations with an average 393-day dwell time; published September 2025 [S5].

diamond.adversary: Microsoft-named China-nexus actor Clay Typhoon (Storm-2416), overlapping Volexity VerdantBamboo, Google UNC5221 and CrowdStrike Warp Panda [S1][S2]; PRC state-sponsored per government BRICKSTORM reporting [S6].
diamond.capability: BRICKSTORM (Linux/ESXi and FreeBSD variants), Junction, GuestConduit, PLENET/GRIMBOLT, AGENTPSD; edge-device and vCenter exploitation; VM snapshot theft and rogue VMs [S1][S3][S6].
diamond.infrastructure: C2 blended into HTTPS/WebSocket with DNS-over-HTTPS resolution [S6]; abuse of compromised MSP access and stolen firewall credentials [S1]. Specific infrastructure indicators not reviewed in this pass.
diamond.victim: US and North American legal, technology/SaaS, BPO, manufacturing, government and IT organizations and MSP customers [S1][S4][S5][S6].
diamond.socioPolitical: Covert long-term access likely supporting PRC strategic intelligence collection, per CrowdStrike [S4]; Google notes possible support to zero-day development and downstream access [S5].
diamond.technology: VMware vCenter/ESXi, Ivanti Connect Secure, F5 BIG-IP, pfSense, Egnyte Storage Sync, network storage and other non-EDR appliances [S1][S3][S5][S6].

gaps: No Microsoft publication describing Clay Typhoon's activity was located; the Microsoft name mapping depends on Volexity reporting relayed by secondary sources [S1][S2].
Microsoft's threat actor naming table (learn.microsoft.com) could not be opened in this pass to confirm the Clay Typhoon / Storm-2416 entry and its listed industry names.

Primary documents not opened: Volexity 'Just Another BRICKSTORM in the Firewall', CrowdStrike Warp Panda blog, Google GTIG BRICKSTORM post, CISA AR25-338A; content relies on search-result summaries and news coverage.
Degree of identity between Clay Typhoon, VerdantBamboo, UNC5221 and Warp Panda is unresolved; GTIG separates UNC5221 from Silk Typhoon [S5].
Sponsoring PRC organization (MSS, PLA or contractor) not identified in located sources.
Exact initial access in the Volexity case is reported inconsistently across secondary summaries.
No MITRE ATT&CK group ID located for Clay Typhoon.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. Step 1 (operational environment): key terrain is the virtualization and appliance layer (vCenter/ESXi, VPN/edge devices, firewalls, storage sync, backup appliances) where EDR is absent [S5][S6], plus MSP trust relationships [S1]. Step 2 (effects): compromise of vCenter permits snapshot theft, credential extraction and hidden VMs, and ADFS key theft enables identity forgery across federated services [S6]. Step 3 (adversary model): patient espionage operator with average dwell above a year, multiple BRICKSTORM variants and fallback implants, and re-entry via stolen credentials after remediation [S1][S5]. Step 4: MLCOA - exploit or reuse credentials on an internet-facing edge device, pivot to vCenter, install BRICKSTORM and quietly collect from DIB-adjacent legal, technology and IT service providers [S3][S5][S6]. MDCOA - leverage MSP or SaaS provider access to reach downstream mission partners, or use ADFS key theft for broad identity compromise [S1][S5][S6]. Candidate indicators: unexpected DNS-over-HTTPS from appliances, new or unregistered VMs, VM clone/snapshot operations outside change windows, vpxuser SSH/SFTP activity, unknown ELF binaries on vCenter/ESXi or FreeBSD firewalls [S3][S6].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. Situational awareness: hypervisor and appliance telemetry is a blind spot that standard endpoint reporting will not cover, so DODIN and partner visibility requests should name vCenter/ESXi, edge, firewall and backup systems explicitly [S5][S6]. Authorities: much exposure lies in contractor, MSP and SaaS environments outside DoD networks, implying coordination through DC3/DIB channels and CISA rather than direct action [S1][S5]. Mission assurance: ADFS key export and vCenter control threaten identity and hosting for mission systems; prioritize key rotation and hypervisor integrity checks after any finding [S6]. Coordination: align with CISA/NSA/Canadian Centre AR25-338A indicators and vendor reporting, recognizing vendors name the activity differently (Clay Typhoon, UNC5221, Warp Panda, VerdantBamboo) [S1][S6].
